articles.author: Raghavi T
articles.description:
CuriousLenz — Making Image Understanding Simple with AI
I'm excited to share CuriousLenz, a web application that lets users upload an image and get an AI-generated explanation.
🔗 Live Demo: https://curiouslenz.vercel.app/
💻 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/raghavit837/curiouslenz
What does CuriousLenz do?
Users can upload an image and ask the application to analyze it. CuriousLenz sends the image to an AI-powered backend and displays the generated response.
Tech Stack
Frontend: React
Backend: Node.js
AI: Groq API with a vision-capable model
Deployment: Vercel and Render
Why I built it
I wanted to build a practical AI-powered web application and learn how to connect a frontend, backend, and AI API into one working product.
Building CuriousLenz helped me understand API integration, deployment, environment variables, and connecting separate services in a production application.
Visit the live demo, upload an image, and see CuriousLenz in action!
I'd love to hear your feedback and suggestions for improving the project.


  
  
  AI #OpenSource #WebDev
articles.title: CuriousLenz: Explore the World Around You with AI 🌿

Merging PDF files sounds like a trivial Sunday afternoon project. Grab file A, grab file B, glue them together, download. How hard could it be?

articles.author: Jiren Edobo
articles.description:
Off-grid solar lighting systems look simple: a solar panel collects energy, a battery stores it, and an LED provides lighting at night.
However, when the system stops working, the problem is usually not caused by one single component. The failure may come from the interaction between power generation, energy storage, control logic, and the final load.
A basic solar lighting system usually works like this:
When troubleshooting, it is important to check the system step by step instead of replacing parts randomly.
The first thing to confirm is the LED load itself. A damaged LED module, internal circuit issue, or loose connection can prevent the light from operating.
If the LED is working properly, the next area to check is the battery. Since the battery stores energy for nighttime operation, reduced capacity, aging, or insufficient charging can cause the system to fail after sunset.
The solar input should then be inspected. Dust, shading, damaged panels, or poor connections can reduce charging performance and gradually lead to nighttime failures.
For outdoor systems, wiring and sensors should also be checked. Exposure to rain, humidity, and temperature changes can cause connection problems over time.
A practical troubleshooting sequence is:
The same approach can be applied to many other off-grid electronic systems. Understanding how energy flows through the entire system is often more effective than focusing on individual components.
Reliable hardware depends not only on good components, but also on proper system integration and maintenance.
articles.title: Debugging an Off-Grid Solar Lighting System: Understanding Common Failure Points

articles.description:
we built a microservice that ingests ~200k events / sec and persists each to a PostgreSQL write‑ahead log (WAL) via libpq batch mode. to avoid a syscall per row we accumulated records in an unbounded in‑memory buffer and flushed only when the buffer hit 1 GB or the process terminated. under realistic load the 99th‑percentile latency jumped from ~2 ms to >200 ms, and tail latency kept growing as the service ran.
unbounded buffering breaks three hard invariants:
memory pressure – the kernel’s dirty‑page throttling (vm.dirty_ratio) triggers writeback pauses once RAM fills, stalling the flush thread and inflating request latency.
fsync latency – a single fsync on a 1 GB buffer must wait for the entire dirty region to be flushed to disk, so any I/O hiccup (e.g. SSD GC) multiplies into a massive…
articles.title: Why Unbounded WAL Batching Kills Latency in High‑Throughput Services

articles.author: StareBrain
articles.description:
There’s a failure mode in on-device AI agents that doesn’t show up in testing.
It shows up five minutes into a real session.
The device gets warm. The CPU downclocks. Latency spikes. The agent that responded in 200ms is now taking 800ms. Users don’t report “thermal throttling” — they report “it got slow” or “it stopped working.”
By the time you’re debugging, it looks like a model problem. It’s not.
What’s actually happening
Android’s thermal system throttles CPU and GPU frequency when the device temperature rises. Continuous inference — running a model repeatedly over several minutes — generates heat. On flagship devices with good thermal management, you might not notice. On a mid-range device from two years ago, you will.
PowerManager.getThermalHeadroom() gives you a 1-second forecast of …
articles.title: Your AI agent works great. Then the phone gets warm. Then it doesn’t.

Open-weight models — models whose trained weights are published for anyone to download — are now good enough for a lot of everyday work: coding agents, tool use, extraction, summarising. The hard part is no longer the model. It is running it. This post covers the three ways to use an open-weight model, what to check before you pick a hosted API, and the few lines of code it takes to call one from the SDKs you already use.
"Open-weight" means the weights are public. It does not automatically mean the training data, the training code or a permissive licence are public too. Licences range from MIT and Apache 2.0 to custom licences with usage limits, so read the model card before you build a product on one. For calling a model through an API, what matters is that anyone can serve it — which is…
